result:
A deadlock is when two or more threads (or processes, or transactions) each hold a resource the other needs and wait forever for the other to release it, so none of them can proceed. The classic case: thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2, while thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1.

It requires four conditions at once: mutual exclusion (the resource can't be shared), hold-and-wait (a thread keeps what it has while waiting for more), no preemption (locks can't be taken away), and a circular wait. Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

The most practical fix is to break the circular wait by always acquiring locks in the same global order everywhere in the code; if every thread takes lock 1 before lock 2, the cycle can't form. Where ordering isn't feasible, acquire with a timeout or try-lock and, on failure, release everything you hold and retry with backoff. Beyond that, hold locks for as short a time as possible, avoid calling unknown code (callbacks, I/O) while holding one, and prefer a single coarse lock or lock-free designs such as message passing or immutable data when you can.

Databases take the remaining route, detection: they find the cycle, abort one transaction as the victim, and expect your code to retry it.
